Overall, I support national election audit standards because I think transparent and credible audits can help people trust election results more. When they are done well, they give the public actual evidence that election outcomes match the ballots that were cast, which is really important at this time. With how divided people are on voting issues right now, having that clarity feels like one of the better ways to strengthen confidence in elections without making voting harder for eligible citizens.

However, one thing I would strongly encourage is a bigger emphasis on language that is simple for the public. I think Audit procedures should help confirm accurate election outcomes without becoming so complicated or burdensome that smaller jurisdictions struggle to carry them out effectively. So, I would encourage election offices to release short public summaries that explain the audit method, what was reviewed, and what conclusions the public should take from it. If people do not understand how the audit works or what the results actually show, it becomes harder for the process to build trust. And I feel like that clear communication matters just as much as technical accuracy. So by doing this, it will further build trust and confidence in voters and eliminate that ambiguity.

Overall, though, I support these proposed standards and encourage the EAC to finalize them in a way that promotes transparency and public trust while still being practical for different states and local election offices.

attributes.comment:
Radical Legibility
To restore the Republic, we must end the era of Administrative Priestcraft and return to a system where the burden of proof is met through Radical Legibility. This is not a step backward into “inefficiency,” but a step forward into Security and Sovereignty.

1. Tearing the Veil
The only way to verify the validity of an election is to remove the digital intermediary. We must replace the proprietary “black box” with a process that is observable by any Citizen without specialized equipment or secret code. A manual, precinct-level hand count is the only method that satisfies the requirement of public proof.

2. Restoring the Master-Servant Relationship
When the count is performed in the light of day by the Neighbors of the Precinct, the government is once again the servant, demonstrating the count to the People. The burden of proof is satisfied in real-time. There is no “crime scene” to be denied entry to, because the Citizen is a witness to the entire process.

3. Verification over Trust
A Constitutional Republic does not ask for “faith” in a machine; it demands verification of the truth. By moving from a hidden “tabulation industry” to a public “tabulation ceremony,” we restore the validity of the count and, by extension, the legitimacy of the government.

attributes.comment:
Both international and national efforts for auditing in the public sector already exist and are well-tested, raising the question of whether the EAC developing audit standards is necessary. The International Organization of Supreme Audit Institutions exists specifically to (among other things) set standards for public sector auditing, and the Government Accountability Office acts as the supreme audit institution for the United States. The GAO is already trusted to provide standards for internal controls on government auditing within federal and state institutions.

This makes the EAC defining these both duplicative and, given the trust deficit in U.S. elections, risky. To successfully define a specific set of auditing standards outside those that are already trusted in other sectors requires a building of trust that would be unnecessary if anchored to existing, respected, and trusted audit standards.

To that end, we recommend the EAC focus on defining the specific needs for the various audits in U.S. elections and not attempt to define broad standards for auditing.

Each candidate who gets at least 10% of the vote in a district with 75,000 or more registered voters should be allowed to select one precinct in that district for an audit.

The audit should include a recount of the paper ballots for that one contest and optionally include an audit of the voters who are on record as having voted in that precinct to ensure they exist and they actually voted.

Comments on Election Audit Standards, Docket EAC-2026-0067
April 27, 2026

Introduction
I have experience in conducting many types of audits, including ISO-9001, ISO 10000, ISO 27001, CMMI-DEV, CMMI-SVC, and Federal government audits of processes, police departments, and research facilities. I have managed Federal ISSO cybersecurity assessments of major IT systems using NIST SP800-53a as a control reference. I have conducted extensive research on US Election Systems, including developing risk management frameworks, work breakdown structures, and security controls to mitigate threats.

Background
The US Election System is comprised of 646 distinct processes covering 57 major areas under the pre-election, election, and post-election major domains. Written procedures for these processes vary from state to state. In order to assess the accuracy of an election, states should use auditing of the election processes, equipment (tabulators and databases), data (ballots and records) and compliance (were the tasks performed correctly). The EAC has developed a draft auditing standard to accommodate the states in federal elections.

Analysis
In order to reduce the risk of errors in federal elections, audits can be prescribed. Different types of audits are required for each major election domain. The domains include: 1. process audit, 2. equipment audit, 3. data audit, 4. compliance audit.
Standards are in place that define the best practices for auditing, including confidentiality, accountability, transparency, timeliness, independence, controls, risk assessment, and remediation. These best practices should be incorporated into the EAC final audit standards.

Recommendations
1. Audit standards should be listed and sortable not only by topic, but by type of audit and by election process sequence (before, during, after election). The standards should be traceable to established auditing standards for the appropriate domain.
2. The auditing process should not be owned by the state CIO, Secretary of State, or Elections Office. It should be a separate entity under the Governor’s office, normally residing in an Inspector General’s office. The authority should be shared by representatives from political parties participating in the election. All auditing processes should be visible to observers from the respective political parties.
3. Auditors should be credentialed in the type of audit being conducted, and experienced in auditing procedures related to elections.
4. Defects discovered in the auditing process should be listed as incidents, and classified as major (affecting the count) or minor (affecting the process). They should be investigated to determine the root cause. The defect should be corrected, and associated processes improved in order to preclude the recurrence of the defect.
5. In order to maintain consistency and identification of issues, auditing of elections should refer to the specific processes involved in accordance with the US election work breakdown structure (WBS) of 646 processes (NIST Election Model of 2019). I can provide a copy of this WBS.

Conclusion
The EAC Election Auditing Guide is a great start to defining a standard set of processes for US federal election audits. The recommendations above can strengthen the guide and ensure a high level of maturity in the auditing processes.

attributes.comment:
1)Objective Standards:
a.Authorization: Is it necessary that an audit be conducted at the direction of the chief election official at the state or local level? What if that official is elected and on the ballot for that election? If the entity is perceived to lack sufficient credibility or capacity, having a senior official who is more insulated from the political process overseeing the audit could be helpful. Additional technical support may be necessary in some cases as well.
b.Funding: Ideally, audits are adequately funded by applicable public resources, but what if there isn’t sufficient public funding to carry them out successfully. Private funding has previously helped successfully administer elections, and there may be a case for allowing private funding if public funding doesn’t come through and there are sufficient safeguards for ensuring that the private financing doesn’t compromise the independent and accountability of the election processes.
c.Impartiality: I might clarify and expound a bit more on this standard. For example, I think I know what you mean when you say that audits must be conducted without bias or prejudice. But everyone has a bit of bias and prejudice, no matter how much they try and keep it in check. I think it’s better to acknowledge this like you further down in the word document, and instead say something like, “Audits must be driven by factual evidence to reach fair and objective conclusions. Relying on things like assumptions, suppositions, or and hearsay is not sufficient.”

attributes.comment:
While election officials are required to comply with election laws, they have considerable discretion over how they manage election operations and how they document the election processes. The internal operations and operating procedures are not transparent despite public records laws. As such, many election officials operate without enough transparency for the public to understand, question and thoughtfully scrutinize election operations.

For decades the operations of public and government entities have been routinely audited by independent outside parties to determine if they do a good job. I am not aware of any election office that is subject to periodic independent audits. As such, the public does not really know if our election offices do a good job. Fair and transparent elections are the fundamental principal on which our Republic was founded. As such, the public deserves to know if election operations are sound and produce reliable results. Making election offices subject to independent audits is necessary and will shine a light on those election officers that do not do a good job.

The EAC’s voluntary standards do not provide for independent audits. When election officials plan, execute and report the results of an audit, it is not an independent audit. Every significant election process should be subject to periodic audits by outside independent parties.

Examples of Some Key Election Processes:

Design of effective internal controls and processes
Adherence to effective internal controls
Documentation of policies and procedures
Processing of voter registration applications
Completeness and accuracy of list maintenance activity
Design and testing of cyber security posture
Processing and tracking of vote-by-mail envelopes and ballots
Aggregation of election results
Reporting of election results
Processing and response to public records requests
Storage and organization of paper ballots

April 26, 2025

Commissioner Donald Palmer
Commissioner Benjamin W. Hovland
U.S. Election Assistance Commission
633 3rd Street NW, Suite 200
Washington, DC 20001

cc: Andrew Sassoon, FOIA Public Liaison
Seton Parsons, Associate Counsel

Dear Commissioners Palmer and Hovland:

On behalf of the Michigan Fair Elections Institute (MFEI), a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization dedicated to election integrity research and public education, I write to express strong support for the proposed changes to the EAC’s audit standards currently under consideration. We urge the Commission to adopt all four of the following reforms.

1.Independent Audit Committee. Administration of election audits should be shifted from entities within the election system to an independent audit committee. Audits conducted by parties with a stake in the outcome cannot command public confidence. Independence is the foundation of credibility.

2.Enhanced County-Level Reporting. Audit standards should require additional reporting on county performance, beyond mere verification of results. Granular, jurisdiction-level data is essential for identifying systemic weaknesses and ensuring accountability at every level of election administration.

3.Full Access to Election Artifacts. Auditors must have access to all election artifacts, with appropriate protections to maintain voter confidentiality. Audits that cannot examine the underlying record are audits in name only.

4. States that receive HAVA grant funding should be subject to substantive, financial audits in compliance with Yellow Book, Generally Accepted Government Accounting Standards (GAGAS). Violators should have their funds clawed back and individuals should be held accountable. See “Part B: Inadequate Scope of Federal Audits Systemic Deficiencies in Government Agency Audits of HAVA grants and an Urgent Request for the Government Accountability Office to Investigate,” MFEI Investigation of Michigan Elections, Sept. 2025, pages 64-70. https://b6d83fed-d9cb-4cb1-9e2f-60cfa1575f8d.filesusr.com/ugd/aa3979_edb360768ac042f0aa5245902b401b52.pdf.

MFEI has conducted extensive comparative research on election administration structures across the states. We have seen firsthand how the absence of independent oversight and complete audit access undermines public trust and leaves systemic vulnerabilities undetected. These four reforms would constitute a meaningful and durable improvement to the national audit standard.

An excerpt from MFEI’s report illustrates the fundamental issues currently plaguing the EAC’s effectiveness:

Two core questions plague the audit of Michigan’s usage of federal HAVA funds.

1. Did federal auditors properly considerstakeholder input about Michigan's election integrity concerns when conducting the $49.88 million HAVA grant audit in 2024? 2. What did the federal auditors do to test whether Michigan's certification was in compliance with all HAVA requirements as required by GAGAS 8.90 and 8.98? It appears the federal auditors focused narrowly on financial compliance under 2 CFR 200 while failing to evaluate critical HAVA mandates, such as voter access, election technology security, voter education, and adequate voter roll maintenance, as required by Titles I and II (52 U.S.C. §§ 20901, 21081).

We thank the Commission for its consideration and encourage prompt adoption of these changes. A strong final standard will provide model language that state legislatures across the country can act upon. Please do not hesitate to contact us if MFEI can provide additional research or testimony in support of this effort.

Respectfully submitted,

Patrice Johnson
Chair and Founder
Michigan Fair Elections Institute
P.O. Box 41
Stockbridge, MI 49285
517-420-7978
patrice@mifairelections.org

attributes.comment:
Introduction:
I am writing this as a semi-retired CPA living in Colorado. I am submitting comments to the EAC in connection with audit standards for elections. Since the meeting in February the EAC has issued a draft document outlining these audit standards and has opened the process for public comment, which I am hereby doing.

Background:
My overall impression of the draft is very positive. The standards you have identified are important and relative to addressing the main purpose of auditing, and that is to increase voters’ trust in elections. I understand that these standards are not necessarily binding at the state level, but issuance of standards by the EAC will provide each state with a good starting point to develop procedures that work for their state laws and specific situation.

I have attached a “redline” copy of your draft document showing my recommended changes, which are few. I urge you to read the edits and consider all of them.

I am highlighting here what I believe is the most important of these changes. My concern has to do with the Objectivity Standard of Independence. I believe independence is the most important standard of all because without proper independence there is no trust. With no trust the entire audit breaks down into a meaningless ceremonial exercise.

Analysis:
The draft document addresses every conceivable issue around independence regarding the folks working directly on the audit. However, it does not deal with the much bigger concern with the party that really controls the audit – the Chief Election Official. Through rulemaking it controls the efficacy, appropriateness, flexibility, confidentiality, security, accountability, and transparency of the audit. These are the very concepts that you have identified to build your standards upon. Your draft document continues to vest the responsibility of all these factors in the hands of this entity. To place the responsibility with the entity that manages elections and also managing the audits of these same elections, creates a conflict of interest or at least a strong perception of one.

Recommendation:
A much better approach would be for each state to set up an independent election commission which could include the state auditor, secretary of state, association of election clerks, CPAs, lawyers, statisticians, consultants, and others to make the rules and high-level decisions that would provide for the kind of independence that really matters.

Conclusion:
Please pay special attention to my comments on pages 5 and 14. If you do nothing else, please accept these changes. This will do more to increase trust in elections than anything else I can think of.

Thank you for considering my request and please let me know if I can be of further assistance.

p.s. - I have also attached a similar proposal being made to the State of Colorado to increase confidence in elections.

attributes.comment: In reading through your document, it appears that you're advocating for Elections Departments to be the ones to audit their elections. Although you label this as a voluntary audit, I think the goal should be that audits be required by law. Even for voluntary audits, the audits should be done by third parties. Third party audits are required in several industries, particularly financial, publicly traded companies and entities receiving certain levels of government grant money. In all these instances, the companies are audited by a third party. In fact, it would seem almost ridiculous to allow them to audit themselves. You mention concerns over sensitive voter data. Auditors for various industries also work with data just as sensitive, if not more sensitive. I do think this is a good idea, but I believe you should stress the confidence that third party audits will provide.

attributes.comment: The Voluntary National Standards for Election Audits – A Practical Guide is an excellent general standards document.  It is deficient in that it doesn't address the specific areas where fraudulent activity is most likely to occur.  There are 4 that I'm aware of; Vote by Mail (VBM), UOCAVA (ballots sent from outside the country), Catching non-citizens at registration and removing non-citizens who are already registered.  Both VBM & UOCAVA currently have insufficient controls.  Areas that should be improved with audit standards include envelop/ballot production and distribution, intake and processing center security, ballot storage security, reconciliation and the need for voter ID inclusion.  For UOCAVA, there is a lack of domestic address control to confirm county address provided is residential and associated with the voter's family.  All 4 ways people can register - with Driver's LIcense (DL), with Social Security number but no DL, No ID and Federal Postcard Application - all need enhanced controls to prevent non-citizens from registering to vote.  Voter roll clean-up guidelines are also needed specifying frequency and methods for identifying and removing non-citizens and inactive voters.

attributes.title: Comment from Citizens Oversight, Inc.

attributes.comment:
I write in strong support of the EAC’s proposed improvements to the Voluntary National Standards for Election Audits and urge the Commission to adopt the four key reforms highlighted by the Michigan Fair Elections Institute (MFEI) in their April 26, 2025 letter (see attached), along with the specific edits proposed by Michael Raisch, CPA.

As a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) with an MBA and over 25 years of experience as a Supervisory Auditor in the Department of Defense, I have conducted and overseen numerous audits performed in full conformance with Generally Accepted Government Auditing Standards (GAGAS / Yellow Book). Independence is not optional under GAGAS—it is foundational. When election officials or entities within the election system audit themselves, the process fails the most basic test of objectivity and public credibility.

I fully endorse:

- Creation of an Independent Audit Committee to administer audits, removing them from any entity with a stake in the outcome.

- Enhanced County-Level Reporting that goes beyond mere verification of results and requires granular performance data on every jurisdiction.

- Full Access to All Election Artifacts for auditors, with appropriate safeguards to protect voter confidentiality. Audits without access to the underlying records are audits in name only.

- Mandatory Substantive Financial and Compliance Audits of HAVA Grant Recipients under GAGAS standards. States that fail to comply with HAVA requirements (including voter roll maintenance, accurate voter histories, and proper use of federal funds) should face immediate suspension, claw-back of funds, and accountability for responsible individuals, exactly as MFEI recommends.

In addition to these reforms, I recommend the standards explicitly require statistical sampling (e.g., random selection of precincts, ballots, voter records, and poll books) as a core audit procedure. Statistical methods provide defensible, representative evidence of systemic issues such as voter roll accuracy, duplicate or outdated registrations, and anomalies in voting history—issues that self-audits by election administrators have repeatedly failed to detect. GAGAS explicitly supports the use of statistical sampling when it is the most efficient and effective way to obtain sufficient, appropriate audit evidence.

The current practice of allowing election officials to audit their own work creates the exact appearance of bias that GAGAS was designed to prevent. The EAC has a historic opportunity to set a national model that restores public confidence by insisting on true independence, complete access, rigorous sampling, and real financial accountability for HAVA funds.

I respectfully urge the Commission to incorporate these changes before finalizing the standards. The Michigan Fair Elections Institute’s attached one-page summary and supporting materials provide concrete examples of why these reforms are urgently needed.

Respectfully submitted,

Mark Vaeth CPA/MBA
Livonia, MI
